terms.comment: The general word, of things and of people alike (see connect for things); the passive, conjungī, to be united.

evidence: Cic. Phil. 4.12: numquam tam vehementer cum senātū cōnsociātī fuistis (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of people joined in a common cause or a partnership; most frequent in Cicero, Livy and Tacitus (Lewis & Short).

terms.grammar: phrase: in + acc., with a verb of gathering or agreeing
evidence: Varr. L.L. 6.43: mēns plūra in ūnum cōgit
terms.comment: Where English says “united” of a group that thinks or acts as one.
Post-Augustan and very rare (Lewis & Short); behind the modern names, as in the United States, but not the word for uniting people.

phrases.latin: tempore quō in homine nōn ut nunc omnia in ūnum cōnsentiant, sed singulīs membrīs suum cuique cōnsilium, suus sermō fuerit
phrases.english: at a time when the parts of a man did not all agree as one, as now, but each limb had its own mind and its own voice

phrases.latin: Ecce quam bonum et quam jūcundum, habitāre frātrēs in ūnum!
phrases.english: Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!

sources: Lewis & Short: conjungo · Lewis & Short: consocio · Lewis & Short: unus · Lewis & Short: unio
